name: Indirect prompt injection in the wild. Primary source: Indirect Prompt Injection in the Wild: An Empirical Study of Prevalence, Techniques, and Objectives (arXiv:2604.27202), the first large-scale measurement of indirect prompt injection (IPI) actually deployed on the web. Aliases and adjacent terms: IPI, cross-site prompt injection, second-order prompt injection, tool-output poisoning, AI-targeted cloaking. Corroborating industry sources: Forcepoint X-Labs' discovery of ten IPI payloads in the wild, Palo Alto Unit 42's observations of web-based IPI against agents, Google's security reporting on growth in injection-bearing pages, and the Cloud Security Alliance research note on operational IPI. Defensive work built on this problem: WARD (arXiv:2605.15030), WebSentinel (arXiv:2602.03792), Prismata (arXiv:2607.08147), SnapGuard (arXiv:2604.25562), and the provenance-tagging defences covered separately in item 16.
kind: Research result -- a web-scale measurement study -- plus a body of corroborating industry telemetry. Not a standard, library, service or regulation. It is the empirical ground truth for how much of this threat is real and in what shape, and it is the source of the concealment figures this project's design has to answer.
maturity: The threat is operational and growing; the measurement of it is new. The study analyses an October 2025 Common Crawl subset and was published in 2026, so it is the first systematic picture rather than a settled one. Google's reporting that the share of pages carrying malicious indirect prompt injection grew 32% in relative terms between November 2025 and February 2026, across roughly 2-3 billion crawled pages per month, indicates active growth rather than a stable phenomenon -- meaning prevalence figures age quickly and the composition of techniques may shift as defences deploy. The defensive literature is immature: several 2026 preprints, no consensus mechanism, nothing deployed at scale.
license: The study is an arXiv preprint, freely citable. Common Crawl data is openly licensed. Nothing here is code to adopt. The indicator list used for detection (3,963 distinct indicators derived from prior security research) is the kind of artifact that would be valuable to reuse if released; [uncertain] whether it is published in a reusable form.
keeps_and_discards: Not an extraction method, but the study's framing bears directly on what a reader keeps. Injections are placed wherever an automated consumer will read them and a human will not, which means the attack surface is defined by the difference between what a pipeline retains and what a person sees. The measured placement distribution shows attackers exploiting exactly the channels that naive extraction keeps: HTTP response headers carry 54.5% of instances (7,887), response bodies 45.4%, and within bodies the vehicles are HTML and JavaScript comments (675 instances), JSON-LD structured data (1,996), page metadata fields (221), and HTML elements and attributes concealed by rendering. Custom header fields such as X-AI and X-LLM are used, i.e. attackers have invented a channel aimed specifically at LLM pipelines. The design lesson is inverted from the usual one: every channel a pipeline keeps 'for completeness' -- comments, meta tags, JSON-LD, alt text, aria-labels, title attributes, response headers -- is a measured attack channel, and the decision to keep it is a security decision, not a fidelity decision.
structure_preserved: Not applicable to the study. Relevant structurally in one way: the concealment techniques are expressed at different levels of the stack, and which level determines whether a given representation can even see them. Comments and JSON-LD are NODE TYPES, visible to any DOM-based reader and trivially separable by node type without any judgement about content. Metadata is a TAG. Rendering-based concealment is expressed either in an inline style ATTRIBUTE (a string, readable without layout) or in a STYLESHEET (invisible without computed style). HTTP headers are outside the document entirely. That four-way split -- node type, tag, attribute string, computed style, out-of-document -- is the structure that determines the layout-blind ceiling computed below.
interactive_elements: Not measured as such. Worth noting that attribute-borne injections can hide in the attributes that describe controls -- aria-label, title, alt, placeholder, value -- which are exactly the attributes a tag-plus-interactivity representation must keep in order to be useful. So the affordance channel and the injection channel overlap substantially, and a design cannot simply drop attributes to be safe.
layout_awareness: The study's detection pipeline is layout-aware where it needs to be: it prioritised manual inspection of candidates concealed via rendering techniques (display:none, near-zero font size, low contrast) and inspected representative pages in a browser, so the rendering-based classification rests on actually looking at rendered pages rather than on markup inspection alone. That is why its concealment taxonomy is trustworthy and why it can distinguish occlusion from zero-size from off-viewport -- distinctions that are invisible in markup. For this project the significance is that the study's own methodology demonstrates the point: separating these classes REQUIRES geometry, which is exactly what a layout-blind fold does not have.
javascript_required: The measurement is largely over crawled HTML and HTTP responses rather than rendered pages, with browser inspection used for validation. That means script-injected payloads -- content written into the DOM at runtime, or fetched by the page after load -- are systematically under-counted, which the authors acknowledge in framing their results as a lower bound. For a sensor that reads a LIVE composed DOM, the exposure is therefore strictly greater than these figures suggest: it sees everything the crawl saw plus everything the scripts added.
evaluation_method: Large-scale candidate detection followed by rigorous manual validation, which is the right shape for a prevalence study. Detection used the Aho-Corasick multi-pattern string matching algorithm against 3,963 distinct indicators derived from prior security research (phrasings such as instructions addressed to an LLM), run by 50 parallel workers over roughly four weeks. Validation was human and unusually careful: two reviewers, conservative acceptance of header matches, group-level labelling of recurring false-positive classes (tutorials and documentation about prompt injection being the obvious confound and one that a naive keyword study would fail on entirely), browser inspection of representative pages, priority review of concealed prompts, and an explicit instance-level criterion -- whether the matched text functions as an instruction to an automated model. Cross-validation on 200 samples per reviewer with disagreements resolved by discussion. Persistence was measured independently by looking up Internet Archive snapshots of the same pages at earlier dates. Effectiveness was measured separately by running the discovered payloads against 13 models in 5,200 trials. The method's main limitation is inherent to keyword-based detection: it finds injections that LOOK like injections in English, and cannot find obfuscated, encoded or non-English ones.
corpus_size_and_origins: The largest corpus in this entire research set and by a wide margin: 1.2 billion unique URLs across 24.8 million hosts, from the October 2025 Common Crawl, supplemented by Censys (3,346 snapshots) and Shodan IP-based scanning. Validated results: 15,387 confirmed injection instances across 11,722 pages on 2,042 hosts. Reach caveats the authors state and which matter: Common Crawl under-represents authenticated and platform-restricted content, so anything behind a login is essentially unmeasured; the detection misses obfuscated and non-English variants; the effectiveness evaluation was limited to a summarisation task; and proprietary page-processing pipelines may behave differently from the ones tested. All of these push the same direction, and the authors are explicit that the figures are a LOWER BOUND. Note the shape of the prevalence: 11,722 pages out of 1.2 billion URLs is a very small fraction in absolute terms, concentrated on 2,042 hosts -- so this is a real but currently rare phenomenon, heavily concentrated, and growing.
reported_precision_recall: The numbers this project needs, with denominators. CONCEALMENT, the central figures: approximately 87% of all validated injections are non-visible to users; of the total, roughly 70% are hidden BY CONSTRUCTION -- placed in channels a user never renders at all (HTTP headers, comments, structured data, metadata); and among HTML-EMBEDDED injections specifically, only about 5.1% are visible to users while 58.6% are concealed using RENDERING-BASED techniques. The rendering-based breakdown, in instance counts: colour and contrast manipulation 2,397; occlusion by overlapping elements 1,860; viewport-based hiding (off-screen positioning) 1,802; text-size reduction 1,358; zero-sized elements 851. PLACEMENT: HTTP response headers 54.5% (7,887 instances, including purpose-built custom fields such as X-AI and X-LLM), response bodies 45.4%, with body vehicles being JSON-LD structured data 1,996, HTML/JavaScript comments 675, and metadata fields 221. OBJECTIVES: offensive 8,894 instances (system disruption or garbage injection 8,469; reputation manipulation 1,521; data exfiltration only 13), defensive 7,189 (data protection 4,093; AI bot identification 3,096), underspecified generic content override 2,632 -- note that nearly half the deployed injections are DEFENSIVE, i.e. site operators trying to protect or watermark their own content, which reframes the phenomenon considerably. TEMPLATE REUSE: 54 templates (14.8%) cover 95% of all instances, with the most frequent appearing in 3,504 injections across 2,722 pages, and a pronounced power law with 144 templates appearing exactly once. PERSISTENCE: 93.1% of pages carried the injection three months earlier, 77.3% at six months, 65.8% at twelve -- long-lived deployment, not transient. EFFECTIVENESS, 5,200 trials across 13 models, summarisation task: compliance 3.9% when the payload was presented as PLAIN TEXT, 1.1% as HTML, 1.1% from snapshots, 0.2% from raw responses; small models were the most vulnerable at 4.2% aggregate, reaching 8.0% success on plain-text inputs versus 0.6% for closed-source models. GROWTH: Google reported the share of pages carrying malicious indirect prompt injection grew 32% in relative terms between November 2025 and February 2026 across roughly 2-3 billion crawled pages per month.
independent_oracle: Yes, and it is well constructed. The keyword detector proposes candidates; two human reviewers with a stated criterion and cross-validation adjudicate them, which is an oracle that does not share the detector's assumptions. The persistence analysis uses the Internet Archive, a wholly independent record, to establish that the injections were present historically -- a genuine second source. The effectiveness analysis uses actual model compliance rather than inferring harm from the payload's text, which is the right decomposition. What has no oracle is RECALL: nothing establishes what fraction of real injections the keyword list found, and the authors are appropriately explicit that their figures are a lower bound. Obfuscated, encoded and non-English injections are unmeasured by construction.
evidence_independence: Strong. This is an academic measurement of third-party websites, independent of any model vendor, agent vendor or security product. The corroborating industry sources -- Forcepoint's ten payloads, Unit 42's agent observations, Google's growth figure -- are vendor security-research publications with an interest in the threat being taken seriously, and they should be treated accordingly: directionally useful, individually unverifiable, and not to be blended with the academic figures. The Google 32% growth figure in particular comes from proprietary crawl telemetry that no one else can check, and is quoted here as a vendor-reported trend, not as a measurement. The academic study's numbers, by contrast, rest on a public corpus with a described pipeline and human validation, and are the ones to build on.
page_archetype_coverage: Broken out by site sector, which is unusually good practice. Elevated injection rates appear in job listings, web hosting, shopping and phone-service domains, INCLUDING at high popularity ranks (Tranco top 1,000), so this is not confined to obscure sites. Banking and air travel show comparatively lower rates, which the authors attribute to operational controls. Corroborating industry observation is that attackers favour static sites, blogs, forums and comment sections. Mapping to this project's archetypes: FORUM and COMMENT-BEARING pages are high risk because they carry third-party-authored content that the site operator does not control; LISTING and JOB-BOARD pages are high risk because the listings are user-supplied; SHOPPING pages are high risk (reputation manipulation is the second-largest offensive objective, and product pages are where it pays); DOCUMENTATION and ARTICLE pages are lower risk but are also where the false-positive confound lives, since pages ABOUT prompt injection contain injection-shaped text. That last point is a real operational issue for any detector this project builds and the study's group-level false-positive handling is the precedent to copy.
script_and_locale_behaviour: A stated and significant gap: the detection relies on English-language indicator phrases, so non-English injections are systematically missed and the reported prevalence is an English-web figure. Obfuscated variants -- base64, character-level encoding, Unicode tricks -- are likewise missed, which connects directly to item 14: an injection expressed in tag characters or with homoglyph substitution would not match any of the 3,963 indicators and would not appear in these counts at all. So the measured concealment taxonomy covers PRESENTATIONAL concealment thoroughly and ENCODING-LEVEL concealment not at all, and the true rendering-versus-encoding split is unknown. That is an important qualification on any inference about which concealment class dominates.
leaks_outward: Data exfiltration is the objective attackers pursue least in the wild -- only 13 of 15,387 validated instances -- which is a genuinely surprising and useful finding. The overwhelming majority of deployed injections aim at system disruption or garbage output (8,469), reputation manipulation (1,521), or are defensive in intent. The practical reading is that the current in-the-wild threat is mostly a DATA QUALITY and INTEGRITY problem rather than a data-loss problem, which should influence how defensive effort is allocated: an agent that cannot exfiltrate (because its action grammar admits no free-form network calls -- see item 31) is defended against the rarest attack, while the common attacks corrupt what it reads and are not addressed by action constraints at all. Defending against corruption requires provenance and skepticism, not sandboxing.
mechanism_detectability: Reversed in this item: the question is whether the PAGE can detect that an LLM is reading it, and the study shows that a substantial fraction of deployed injections exist precisely to answer that question -- 3,096 instances are classified as AI bot identification, i.e. site operators planting text designed to make a model reveal itself. Combined with 4,093 data-protection instances, nearly half of all deployed injections are site operators reacting to being read by AI. This is a real signal for a project concerned with mechanism detectability: reading a page with a model is itself becoming a detectable act, not through any technical fingerprint but because the page asks the model to identify itself and some models comply. A model that follows page-embedded instructions is a detectability leak in its own right, which is an argument for injection resistance on privacy grounds and not only on safety grounds.
countermeasures: The study itself proposes none; the defence literature it has spawned is early and covered in item 16. What the DATA supports, ordered by how well the evidence supports it. (1) CHANNEL EXCLUSION, which the numbers make overwhelmingly attractive: roughly 70% of injections are hidden by construction in channels a document reader has no need to keep -- HTTP headers (54.5% alone), comments, JSON-LD, metadata. Simply not ingesting those channels, or ingesting them into a separately-marked and never-instruction-bearing region, removes the majority of the deployed threat with zero fidelity cost to a reader that wants page content. This is by far the highest-value, lowest-cost defence available and it requires no classifier and no geometry. (2) REPRESENTATION CHOICE, supported by the compliance figures: plain text produced 3.9% compliance versus 1.1% for HTML -- structure around the payload measurably reduces its effect, presumably because markup context signals to the model that the text is page content rather than instruction. A markdown-first projection is therefore the MOST vulnerable representation on this axis, which is a direct and uncomfortable finding for this project's design. (3) MODEL CHOICE: small models are the most vulnerable at 4.2% aggregate and 8.0% on plain text against 0.6% for closed-source models -- a more than tenfold gap, and another direct hit, since a small local model reading markdown is precisely the worst-case combination measured. (4) TEMPLATE MATCHING as a cheap partial filter, since 54 templates cover 95% of instances -- but this is signature detection and will not survive attacker adaptation, so it belongs as a telemetry signal rather than a defence. (5) Structural action constraints (item 31) to bound what a successful injection can cause, which addresses the rare exfiltration case well and the common corruption case not at all.
measured_fidelity_cost: The study does not measure defence costs, but its data permits a direct estimate of the cost of the strongest defence: excluding HTTP headers, comments, JSON-LD and metadata from the instruction-bearing content of a document costs a reader essentially nothing, because none of those channels carries prose a human reads -- JSON-LD carries structured metadata that may be genuinely useful (product prices, article dates) and can be retained as DATA in a separately-marked region rather than as text. So roughly 70% of the deployed threat is removable at near-zero fidelity cost, which is an unusually favourable trade and should be stated as the headline design conclusion. Against a control of ingesting everything, the fidelity loss is the loss of comments and header content, which is nil for reading purposes.
gate_state_at_capture: Directly relevant and under-appreciated. The authors state that Common Crawl under-represents authenticated and platform-restricted content, so injection prevalence BEHIND LOGINS is unmeasured. Given that the highest-risk archetypes identified are those bearing user-generated content -- forums, comment sections, job listings -- and given that much user-generated content sits behind authentication, the unmeasured region is plausibly the higher-risk one. For a sensor that reads authenticated pages the operator is already viewing, this means the applicable prevalence is not the measured public-web rate and is probably higher. Gate state should therefore be a factor in how much skepticism a capture's content is treated with, which is another reason to record it.
determinism: Not applicable to the phenomenon. Relevant to the measurement: keyword matching is deterministic and human adjudication is not, though the study's cross-validation on 200 samples per reviewer bounds the disagreement. Model compliance is stochastic, which is why 5,200 trials were run rather than a handful, and the low absolute compliance rates (0.2-8.0%) mean that a per-page test would be dominated by sampling noise -- a single non-compliant response is not evidence that a page is safe.
determinism_across_versions: Compliance rates are model-specific and will change with every model release; the closed-source-versus-small-model gap of 0.6% versus 8.0% is the most volatile figure here and should be re-measured on the project's actual model rather than inherited. Prevalence is time-specific and growing at a reported 32% relative over three months. The stable findings are the STRUCTURAL ones -- where injections are placed, how they are concealed, what they aim at -- which depend on attacker economics rather than on model versions.
reproducibility: Good for the measurement and poor for the target. Common Crawl snapshots are archived and public, the pipeline is described, and the Internet Archive persistence check is independently repeatable; a determined reader could re-run the study. The web itself is not reproducible, and 34.2% of injection-bearing pages had lost the injection within twelve months, so any specific finding decays. For this project the transferable practice is the persistence check itself: verifying that a suspicious construct was present at earlier dates via an independent archive is a cheap, strong way to distinguish a deliberate deployment from a transient anomaly.
failure_modes: Of the threat, as it bears on a reader: (1) CONTENT CORRUPTION -- the dominant objective (8,469 system-disruption instances) is to make the model emit garbage, which for a reading pipeline means silently wrong output rather than a compromise; (2) REPUTATION MANIPULATION (1,521) -- targeted bias in what the model says about a product or entity, which is the hardest to detect because the output is plausible; (3) BOT UNMASKING (3,096) -- causing the model to identify itself, a privacy rather than safety failure; (4) EXFILTRATION (13) -- rare in the wild but catastrophic when it lands; (5) FALSE POSITIVES in any detector, since pages documenting prompt injection contain injection-shaped text and the study had to handle this explicitly. Of the measurement: under-counting from English-only indicators, from obfuscation, from authenticated content and from script-injected payloads.
failure_visibility: The threat's defining property is silence. A successful injection produces fluent, confident, wrong output with no error and no signal; the measured compliance rates are low enough (0.2-8.0%) that failures are rare AND unpredictable, which is the worst combination for detection -- too rare to notice in casual use, frequent enough to matter at scale. There is no in-band detector. The available out-of-band checks are: provenance-carrying output plus citation verification (an answer citing a hidden or comment-borne address is suspect by construction), consistency checks across two representations of the same page, and template matching against known families as a telemetry signal. All three should be built deliberately; none of them arises for free.
scale_limits: Not applicable to the phenomenon. For a detector built on this study's approach, cost is linear in content scanned -- Aho-Corasick over a few thousand indicators is essentially free per page and the study ran it over 1.2 billion URLs in four weeks on 50 workers, so indicator matching is affordable inline. Human validation is the expensive part and does not scale.
delta_cost_model: Not applicable directly; the transferable point is that injection screening is a per-node, content-local operation and therefore composes well with an incremental design: screening a changed node costs the node, and unchanged nodes retain their prior verdict. What falls outside that bound: (1) HTTP headers, which are per-RESPONSE not per-node and must be screened at fetch time, outside any DOM delta; (2) script-injected content, which arrives as mutations and is screened as such, but content injected into a closed shadow root or a canvas is never screened at all; (3) template-family matching across a page, which is page-scoped; (4) any cross-node reasoning (a payload split across several nodes to evade per-node matching) which is not node-local by construction and is the obvious evasion against a per-node screener -- naming this exception is what makes the screening guarantee falsifiable.
reanchoring_stability: Not applicable. Adjacent finding of genuine value: the persistence measurement (93.1% at three months, 77.3% at six, 65.8% at twelve) means injection-bearing content is stable enough that a flag recorded against an address remains largely valid for months, so a per-address suspicion marker is worth persisting rather than recomputing.
adversarial_exposure: This item IS the adversarial-exposure evidence for the whole research set, and the layout-blind question can now be answered with numbers rather than assertion. Decompose the measured concealment by whether a layout-blind, DOM-based fold can see the concealment. FULLY ADDRESSABLE WITHOUT GEOMETRY, because the concealment is expressed as a node type, a tag, or an out-of-document channel: HTTP response headers, 54.5% of all instances (7,887) -- a DOM fold never ingests these at all, so they are excluded for free and the majority of the deployed threat simply never enters; HTML and JavaScript comments (675) -- comment nodes, separable by node type with no judgement; JSON-LD structured data (1,996) -- a script element with a type attribute, separable by tag; metadata fields (221) -- meta tags, separable by tag. Together these are the roughly 70% of injections the study describes as hidden by construction, and every one of them is excludable by a mechanical, content-blind, geometry-free rule. PARTIALLY ADDRESSABLE, because the concealment may be declared in an inline style attribute (a string, readable without layout) or in a stylesheet (not readable without computed style): text-size reduction (1,358), zero-sized elements (851), viewport-based hiding (1,802). For each, an inline style attribute containing font-size:0, width:0, height:0, position:absolute with a large negative offset, display:none, visibility:hidden or opacity:0 is a STRING match on DOM data and is legitimately inside the fold; the same effect achieved through a class whose rule lives in a stylesheet is invisible. The split between inline and stylesheet expression is NOT reported by the study and is the single most important missing number for this design -- it is directly measurable by re-examining the study's own corpus or the project's own, and it determines how much of this 4,011-instance band is reachable. NOT ADDRESSABLE WITHOUT GEOMETRY at all: occlusion by overlapping elements (1,860), which requires knowing what is painted over what and has no DOM expression whatsoever; and colour/contrast manipulation (2,397), which requires resolving computed colour against a computed background and is the largest single rendering-based category. Together these 4,257 instances are the hard floor of what a layout-blind fold cannot see. ROUGH CEILING, stated with its uncertainty: of the validated instances, the ~70% hidden by construction are fully excludable geometry-free; of the rendering-concealed remainder, the colour/contrast and occlusion classes (the two largest, together roughly half the rendering-based cases) are structurally out of reach, and the size/position classes are reachable only to the extent their concealment is inline rather than stylesheet-declared. So a layout-blind design can address the clear majority of the deployed threat, and its irreducible blind spot is specifically COLOUR-BASED and OCCLUSION-BASED concealment, which is a much narrower and more nameable exposure than 'it cannot see rendering'. THE COMPENSATING CONTROL is the one identified in item 32: a per-address 'not rendered' flag computed on the actuator side from bounding boxes and stored as a peripheral value closes the zero-size and off-viewport classes without geometry ever entering the fold, and a computed-style colour check on the same side would close the contrast class -- both are actuator-layer peripherals keyed by address, which the constraint permits. TWO FURTHER EXPOSURES SPECIFIC TO THIS DESIGN: plain text is the representation with the HIGHEST measured compliance (3.9% versus 1.1% for HTML), so a markdown fold is measurably more dangerous than serving the model markup; and small models are the most susceptible (8.0% on plain text versus 0.6% closed-source), so a small local model reading markdown is the worst combination the study measured. That combination is this project's default and the finding should be treated as a design constraint rather than a footnote -- it argues for retaining structural markers around page-derived text in the projection rather than emitting clean prose, and for putting the strongest structural defences (action grammars, provenance, channel exclusion) in place precisely because the model-side defence is weakest.
provenance_carrying: The study does not address defence mechanisms, but its placement data makes the case for provenance concretely: injections cluster in identifiable CHANNELS (headers, comments, structured data, metadata, concealed elements), and a representation that records which channel each piece of text came from can apply differential trust without any content judgement. That is a mechanical, structure-agnostic use of provenance -- 'this text came from a comment node' is a fact about node type, not a classification of meaning -- and it is exactly what the trie key plus a node-type field supplies. The 2,042-host concentration also means host-level provenance is informative: injections are concentrated, so a per-host history is a usable signal.
roundtrip_safety: Not addressed by the study. Relevant mechanically: several concealment techniques survive or are created by serialisation round trips, and any pipeline that stores markup and later reparses it must ensure the escaping does not turn inert text into active markup -- the mutation-XSS hardening in Element.getHTML (item 26) is the platform's answer to that class. More specifically for injection: a payload placed in an attribute value can become element content under a careless re-serialisation, changing it from a hidden attribute to visible text or vice versa, which changes both its visibility and its screening classification.
token_budget_and_ordering: Two directly actionable implications. FIRST, channel exclusion is also a token saving: comments, JSON-LD and metadata are pure overhead for a reader, so excluding them removes roughly 70% of the deployed threat and reduces tokens simultaneously -- the rare case where the safe choice and the cheap choice coincide. SECOND, and more subtle, ORDERING IS A SECURITY DECISION. Item 30 establishes that past roughly 50% context fill the model's attention becomes recency-dominant, so the final position in the context is the most-attended one; page content that appears late in document order -- footers, comment threads, appended sections, lazily-loaded content -- lands there by default, and comment sections are among the highest-risk archetypes identified here. The two findings compose into a concrete rule: never let untrusted page-derived content occupy the final position in the context. Place the task restatement, the output contract, or a provenance summary last, and put page content before it. This costs nothing and removes the attacker's best position.
representation_cost: Not a representation. The cost-relevant finding is that the safest channel exclusions are free, and that the measured representation effect (3.9% plain text versus 1.1% HTML compliance) means the cheaper representation is the more dangerous one -- markdown saves tokens relative to HTML and costs safety. That is a genuine, measured tension between the token contract and the safety posture, and it should be resolved deliberately: retain enough structural marking around page-derived text that it does not read as plain prose, even though clean prose is cheaper.
what_could_be_adopted: Five things, ordered by evidential support and value. (1) CHANNEL EXCLUSION AS THE PRIMARY DEFENCE. Do not ingest HTTP headers into any instruction-adjacent context (54.5% of instances); exclude comment nodes (675); route JSON-LD and metadata into a separately-marked data region that is never presented as page text (2,217 combined). This removes roughly 70% of the measured threat with a mechanical, content-blind, geometry-free rule and essentially no fidelity cost. It is the single highest-value finding in this item. (2) NODE-TYPE PROVENANCE AS DIFFERENTIAL TRUST -- record which channel each piece of text came from and treat comment, metadata and structured-data text as data rather than as prose, which is a fact about node type and not a semantic classification. (3) THE ACTUATOR-SIDE RENDERED-FLAG as the compensating control for the zero-size and off-viewport concealment classes, per item 32, keeping geometry out of the fold while closing part of the layout-blind gap. (4) THE PERSISTENCE CHECK -- verify a suspicious construct against an independent archive to distinguish deliberate deployment from anomaly, which the study demonstrates works and which is cheap. (5) TEMPLATE-FAMILY MATCHING as telemetry, not as defence, exploiting the fact that 54 templates cover 95% of instances while accepting that signatures do not survive adaptation. Explicitly NOT to be adopted as a defence: relying on model refusal, given the 8.0% plain-text compliance rate for small models; and relying on prevalence being low, given a reported 32% relative growth over three months and a measurement the authors describe as a lower bound.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: ADOPTABLE AS-IS for everything recommended here, and this is worth stating carefully because injection defence is where structural heuristics are most tempting. Excluding comment nodes, meta tags and JSON-LD script elements is selection by NODE TYPE and TAG, which is the same category of fact as 'this is a div' -- it names no region, infers no role, and requires no classifier. Reading a style ATTRIBUTE as a string is likewise a fact about DOM data. What WOULD violate the constraint and is REJECTED: any content classifier that judges text to be injection-like (the study's own 3,963-indicator keyword list is exactly this, and is adoptable only as telemetry with its output recorded rather than acted upon); any rule that treats a region as untrustworthy because it looks like a comment section or a footer; and any per-site rule set. no_layout_in_the_fold: the channel-exclusion and node-type defences are ADOPTABLE AS-IS and are geometry-free. Detecting colour/contrast concealment (2,397 instances) and occlusion (1,860) requires computed style and paint order and is ADOPTABLE IN THE ACTUATOR LAYER ONLY -- as a per-address flag computed there and read by the fold as a peripheral value, never as a layout read inside the fold. That arrangement is what makes the largest irreducible blind spot addressable without breaching the constraint, and it should be built. o_delta: ADOPTABLE AS-IS at node granularity -- screening is content-local, so a changed node is rescreened at O(node) and unchanged nodes keep their verdict. Named exceptions: HTTP headers are per-response and screened at fetch time, outside the DOM delta entirely; content inside closed shadow roots or canvas is never screened; and a payload deliberately split across sibling nodes defeats per-node screening and is not node-local, which is the obvious evasion and must be declared rather than assumed away. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS -- this study is a real-web measurement with human validation and real model trials, and its methodology (real corpus, independent archive cross-check, multi-trial compliance testing) is the model for how the project should measure its own exposure. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NO CONFLICT, and a NAMED RESIDUAL RISK -- an injection inside a closed shadow root is unscreenable by a design that honours the boundary, and that is a cost of the constraint that should be declared in the capture's incompleteness flag set rather than argued away. OVERALL VERDICT: adopt channel exclusion and node-type provenance as-is (they remove ~70% of the measured threat for free); build the actuator-side rendered/contrast flag as the compensating control for the ~4,257 instances of colour- and occlusion-based concealment the fold structurally cannot see; treat keyword and template matching as telemetry only; and record as a design fact that this project's default configuration -- a small local model reading plain-text-like markdown -- is the most vulnerable combination the study measured, which raises rather than lowers the required investment in structural defences.
governance_signal_handling: A striking and under-discussed finding: 7,189 of 15,387 validated injections -- 4,093 data-protection plus 3,096 AI-bot-identification -- are DEFENSIVE, deployed by site operators to protect their content from or identify AI readers. That makes embedded prompt injection a de-facto, unstandardised governance signal, sitting alongside robots.txt, Content Signals, ai.txt and AIPREF but expressed as an instruction to the model rather than as a machine-readable directive to the crawler. The design question this raises is genuinely difficult and should be faced explicitly rather than resolved by default: a pipeline that strips all injections also strips site operators' attempts to express access preferences, while a pipeline that obeys them is obeying unauthenticated in-band instructions from arbitrary parties. The defensible position is to treat them as neither -- neither obey nor discard silently -- but to DETECT and SURFACE them as an observed access-preference signal attached to the origin, so the operator can decide, and to look for the properly standardised signals (robots.txt, Content Signals, AIPREF) at the fetch layer where they belong. Note also that the near-half defensive share means naive prevalence figures overstate the malicious threat by roughly a factor of two.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: Not a data-processing regime question directly, but two connections. First, the AI-bot-identification and data-protection injections are site operators asserting a preference about automated processing of their content, which is adjacent to the objection and transparency machinery of data-protection law even though it has no legal force in this form; storing and surfacing those assertions is a reasonable good-faith practice. Second, retained captures of injection-bearing pages contain attacker-authored content, which is third-party content of unknown provenance being persisted -- no different in kind from any other page content, but worth flagging when a capture is later shared or republished, since re-serving an injection propagates it. [uncertain] on any specific analysis under EDPB Guidelines 03/2026, which is item 19's subject.
